Question: How do names work in sign language?
items.raw: Sign language finger spelling isn't really like fingerspelling in English, I would say, it's less constrained by the alphabet, it's more phonetic or phonemic, you spell out the sounds of the name rather than the letters, so a name like Helen might be spelled H E L E N in English fingerspelling, in sign language you would probably spell something like HAY LEN, or maybe just HAY LEN, it depends on the pronunciation, and it doesn't really matter that much, the idea is just to approximate it, but then names that sound nice, like Mary, they can have a sign, they can have a name sign, and that's just a single handshape and a single movement, or a handshape held still, it's just a reference, it's like a nickname, and it's very quick and efficient, it's like calling somebody by their initials in English, but the sign isn't fixed, people make up their own name signs, sometimes people fight about name signs, but generally it's just an ad-hoc reference sign.

Question: Who is the USA so in debt to?
items.raw:
Glad your initial question life drafted me
So in brief it is the Japanese Government then the UK Government then China but they hold like 30 percent and the rest is spread across many countries and institutions and central banks. There is also private debt which is debt to Americans themselves, pension funds, mutual funds, banks, insurance companies, foreign central banks, foreign sovereign funds, foreign private investors, corporations, households. So it is all sorts of things. And when you say debt I'm assuming you mean Treasury bills or Treasury bonds which are short term and long term government debt.
Anyway, there is lots of debt and it is held by lots of people. As a rule of thumb the holder is always someone who is going to pay their debt. So banks will hold some Treasury bills, because it's a safe asset. They can use it as collateral, as security for other transactions. So it's a nice asset to have. The US is a very powerful country, it's a very stable country, so its debt is a very safe asset. So everyone likes to hold some of it. It's just like the money that you put in the bank. You're lending money to the bank in a way.

Question: Who is the USA so in debt to?
items.raw:
Hi Spud,

What you are asking about is how the federal government borrows money. When there is a deficit, the treasury goes to the market and asks for a loan, which is put up as a bond. These bonds can be bought by anyone, individuals, corporate organisations, funds and banks, foreign governments, and US state and local governments, even foreign individuals. So its not clear who the US is in debt to. However, its the US treasury and the Fed who buy the most US bonds. So its more correct to say the US is in debt to itself. But Chinese, Japanese, UK, etc governments have large holdings. If China was to sell off all their US debt, it would be a crisis. Because its impossible for China to buy anything else in large volumes, it would put too much downward pressure on the dollar. But the debt to other countries is more stability than danger. Its part of the reason that the dollar is the global reserve currency.

Regards

Humph

items.raw: Here's my experience with it. And well, judges and agencies in all jurisdictions seem to like it because it's simpler to compute. Everybody makes it simpler in law and rules and regulations. So rather than have a case by case analysis of what's the needs of the child, do we have a formula that can be computed in minutes rather than hours, days, weeks? So the formula of course is, what's the income, what's the percentage, what's the number of children? Now the problem with that is, the formula doesn't take into account the needs of the child. So if you have a child who needs a lot of medical expenses, or is very expensive to take care of, then the formula is not going to be enough. And then the parents have to go to court to get a modification or an adjustment to the child support.

Question: why child support is based on income rather than what a child would need monthly.
items.raw: I think these are essentially the same thing from a policy standpoint. We can argue the numerology a lot but the aim of a child support scheme is to ensure that the parent has the funding to cover the required costs of raising a child. And therefore you would aim to have the parent at some percentage of the income they have to pay, or the child at some percentage of the income of the household as if the child were still in it. Now, you could argue the other way about what would it cost to raise a child. But in practice, the household income is going to be a better predictor of the cost of raising a child in that household than trying to say, we should just say a child is worth $1,000 a month and everybody should pay that. That's not going to work very well, because the cost of raising a child varies wildly based on the cost of living in the region and the standard of living of the household.

At 3:12 every Thursday morning, Mara found the book in the bread rack.

It was always the same one: The Practical Guide to Inland Birds, cracked blue spine, library stamp from a town forty miles away. She would set it on the flour bin, wipe butter from the cover, and mean to take it back after her shift. By noon, the errands and heat and sleep would swallow the thought.

Then, next Thursday, there it would be again, tucked between cooling rye loaves.

Tonight the bakery hummed with the proofing cabinet and the old radio’s static. Rain pressed silver lines down the front window. Mara lifted the book with both hands, as if it might be warm.

A folded receipt marked the chapter on herons.

She opened it.

In block letters, someone had written: I THINK YOU ARE THE ONLY PERSON AWAKE WHEN I AM. PAGE 47.

Mara turned to page 47. A grey heron stood in a marsh, one foot raised, patient as a saint. Under the picture, in pencil: THURSDAY, 3:30?

The clock over the mixer clicked once.

Mara brushed flour from her apron, unlocked the front door, and turned on the little OPEN sign.

A simple rain gauge measures rainfall by catching precipitation in a funnel and directing it into a cylindrical measuring tube. 

To ensure accurate and easy reading, the gauge's top opening is deliberately wider than the inner measuring tube. This difference in diameter acts as an amplifier. For example, if the collection opening has ten times the area of the inner tube, one inch of rainfall will fill the tube to a height of ten inches. This magnification allows observers to easily and precisely read very small amounts of rainfall, such as hundredths of an inch.

However, these instruments are subject to errors. One common source of inaccuracy is evaporation; collected water can quickly evaporate before it is measured, especially in warm or windy weather. Another major source is wind exposure. Strong winds can create turbulence around the gauge's mouth, carrying raindrops over the opening and causing the instrument to underestimate the actual rainfall.

Question: Why is the USA drinking age set at 21 when in most other respects you're an adult at 18.
items.raw: I disagree that there’s a full consensus of why laws enforce 21. But there are some reasons. Insurance and road safety culture put enormous weight on data. There’s tons of empirical data and data also suggests that risk goes down significantly after 21. The insurance industry was very, very heavily involved in lobbying for the highway drink promotion scheme. So it’s one of those things where, once it’s established at the federal level and there’s a funding incentive state by state, it’s hard to un-establish it. And then of course there’s cultural reasons. In many countries, they wait to let young people drink alcohol until they’re already in the labour market. In the UK, they tend to drink young, but in many other countries, they wait until you’re 18, or even 20. And part of it is that once you’re in the labour market, your social circle changes. You’re less likely to have those culture of binge drinking and peer pressure situations, you’re more likely to drink responsibly. So, culturally, we just decided to do it here. There’s another reason, which is that prior to the introduction of the national drink promotion scheme, the drinking age was really all over the place state by state. Some states were 18, some were 20, some were 21. And they wanted to put it on an even footing. So it was a question of, does it make sense to standardise it at 18, at 20, or at 21? And the reasons why they chose 21 were the insurance data, and also the cultural decision to keep young people away from alcohol as long as possible.

Question: What's the difference between tornadoes, hurricanes, cyclones, typhoons etc?
items.raw:
Here's a brief rundown of tornadoes, hurricanes, cyclones, typhoons etc.

We define a storm (or cyclone) as an area of low pressure and inward spinning winds. So hurricanes, typhoons and cyclones are all the same thing, different words. A cyclone is a storm which forms in the southern hemisphere, or in the northern hemisphere over the Indian Ocean. So a cyclone is not necessarily a sea storm, it could also be over land. A hurricane is a cyclone in the Atlantic Ocean and Gulf of Mexico in the northern hemisphere. Typhoon is a cyclone in the western Pacific Ocean. So the difference is just where in the world the storm forms. The word tornado on the other hand, is something completely different.

Tornadoes are air storms that are not necessarily connected to storms or cyclones. So a tornado is a very concentrated column of air which spins extremely rapidly. It gets classified as a tornado when the column of air actually touches the ground. So in a tornado, the winds can get to speeds of over 400 kilometres per hour. So they're much faster than a hurricane, but they only affect a very small area. And the funnel shape of a tornado doesn't necessarily go all the way down to the ground. So if it's in the air, we call it a funnel cloud, and it's only a tornado when it touches the ground. And tornadoes form a lot more often than hurricanes or cyclones. So, in the US, there's about 1,200 tornadoes a year. So it's much more common than hurricanes, but the energy in a tornado is much less than in a hurricane, because it affects a much smaller area. So a hurricane is a very large storm. The winds can get up to about 300 kilometres per hour, but the area affected is much larger. So a tornado is like a laser beam, a hurricane is like a light bulb.

Question: What's the difference between tornadoes, hurricanes, cyclones, typhoons etc?
items.raw:
Tornadoes are essentially large smoke-precipitates of compressed air taken from the clouds. They form from the force of a storm clouds of water vapor, which charge electrically as they travel through electrical storms and cold air. Tornadoes take in a whole balloon of vortex with wide tapered tip up top and a little horn of micro vortex with fine taper coming out the bottom.

Hurricanes and cyclones and typhoons are all names to describe a particular type of storm system. These storms form in rotating belts of moist air, called ITZs, intertropical convergence zones, which lie around the equator. As the air rotates, due to the Coriolis force, these zones are the belts of air that go into a storm system like hurricanes and cyclones. And all these names are just location names. In the Atlantic, we call these hurricanes. In the Pacific, we call them typhoons. In the Indian Ocean, we call them cyclones. They all mean the same thing. A hurricane is a rotating vortex storm system that is set off the equator and develops over moist tropical waters. They form from what we call a tropical disturbance, which is a disorganized patch of thunderstorms and heavy rains and low pressure. If these disturbances are given enough energy, they form into something called a tropical depression, which is like a large thunderstorm system, an organized thunderstorm system. So it has rotation, it has rain, it has a low pressure center. And then when that system starts to intensify and spin up more, we call it a tropical storm. And when a tropical storm's winds reach hurricane speed, which is 74 miles per hour, we call it a hurricane. So it's just an issue of the wind speed. And it's also an issue of the location where it's happening, because you call it a hurricane in the Atlantic, a typhoon in the Pacific, and a cyclone in the Indian Ocean.

Question: Can someone explain Post-Modernism like I'm 5, please?
items.raw:
Is there such thing as the truth? Lets say I dreamt about a cake in my dream. I woke up, and it was gone. My mum says "you have to eat food from the shop, not just dreamt food, it's not real". So the cake is not real. But in the dream, the cake was real. I ate it, it tasted good. So the cake was real. Now, is the truth, the cake or the memory of the cake? That is a post modern question. Post modernism says that there is not really truth, but a story. And it's the same truth for everyone. It's a joke on truth. Like if i write a story about France in the 1800s, it doesn't really matter how it really was, it's just me, telling my story of France in the 1800s. The post modern will tell you "come on, isn't it funny that we just have no truth, all of history is made up of stories, and it's up to us to make meaning out of them." The cake wasn't real, but the joke of the cake still happened. And now we need to come up with something funny out of all this confusion.

You would tell your grandad in his chair in the living room about a specific event in his life, and he would say, no it wasn't like that, it was different, it was exactly like this. But for the post modern, it's also true. We may have objectivity, but we have subjectivity as well. And post modern says maybe its more interesting to dive into subjectivity and why do we lie to ourselves? The joke is, we lie to ourselves on purpose, to make our lives better. Or to make money. And that is why its about critique. Its about finding the silly side of a narrative, maybe in politics, and say, come on, that's just nonsense, that's not how the world is, you are telling me an easy story, that doesn't work. I will deconstruct your story and make you more aware of your own lies. And that is post modernism.

Question: Theoretically, shouldn't a pyramid scheme work?
items.raw:
Quotas actually just reward early investors
If everyone joined a pyramid scheme in time then their quota would hit and they'd be rewarded with revenue.
But the issue is it doesn't work in practice because no one joins in time. So you run out of potential customers and the late joiners don't reach their quotas.

So on a day-to-day basis, its actually quite efficient at passing risk down the line. Anyone joining later, takes on greater risk, and anyone who joins earlier is hedged with less risk.

Question: Theoretically, shouldn't a pyramid scheme work?
items.raw: What’s copping many people on intro to pyramid schemes is that it looks mathematically sound. But on the face of it, a few issues make it collapse. First, in a pyramid, you need more and more people coming in at each level to support the ones at the top. So you need an exponential growth in membership. And unless the scheme finds membership close to the whole population of the planet, it’s going to run out of people. That’s the main issue, but then on top of that, there’s a liquidity issue. So most pyramids promise you a really attractive return on your investment. But in order to pay the guys on top, they need to pay them on time. And if there’s a point at which it needs to stop, then they’ll run out of liquidity and just be unable to pay everybody.

items.raw: What’s funny is many people are surprised Windows actually has the capability to do this without sending data to the driver. Winamp doesn’t use the driver in the least when it’s generating those lovely old 3D stereograms, it just feeds those little time domain and frequency domain data streams and then does the processing itself. So the data goes from the source, gets decoded, and then it’s just like an array of little floating point numbers. And Winamp does the calculations. All those 3D ones are just maths. So the numbers are mapped to vertices in a 3D space, and then it draws them. And it’s just an OS API call to draw some polygons. So it’s a bit of geometry and a bit of maths. And yeah, very hard to do it well, especially just to look pretty and stylised. So it’s all maths, and you have to really know your maths if you want to make it look good. But it’s just maths. Some of the visualizations are like those psychedelic blobs, it’s just maths. There’s no DSP involved. So it’s just, okay, we’ve got frequencies, or frequencies and amplitudes. And then it’s just a bunch of lines. And we just move them around in space. And then render them. And just drawing it in a window is actually very expensive. So Winamp is quite expensive to render a screen full of 3D graphics on a computer in the nineties, and even now if you really crank it up. So it’s maths and rendering, and no DSP. So, no real DSP involved. It’s just getting the data out of the audio stream, and then doing some maths and some drawing. And if you want to do it in real time on a computer, it’s quite a bit of maths, and there’s not really any other way to do it. You could maybe do it with the driver, but it’s just easier to do it in Winamp. And actually, it’s easier to do it in pure software.
